## 1 · Project Overview

This report documents the complete, reproducible ML pipeline built on **Lartisien Collection** luxury hotel rate data — rebuilt as v2 with 24 Lartisien-verified hotels and interpretable features.

> **Business question:** Can we tell a Lartisien Voyager traveller when a property enters a low-demand window — lower price, higher availability, more space and privacy — for a given hotel, month, and room type?
>
> **Task 1 — Classification:** Is a given hotel + room + month combination *Premium* (rate > €3,000/night) — a proxy for a high-demand, low-availability period — or *Standard*, a proxy for a quieter, more accessible one?
>
> **Task 2 — Regression:** What is the estimated nightly rate in EUR, so the price gap between visiting in-season vs. off-season is concrete, not just a tier label?

**Dataset v2:** 1,440 rows · 24 Lartisien-verified hotels · 6 room categories · 10 sample dates per room/hotel.
**Random seed:** `random_state=42` everywhere; `np.random.seed(42)` above.
**Leakage:** All preprocessing inside `sklearn.Pipeline`, fitted on X_train only.
**From proposal to v2:** the approved Phase 1 proposal (10 hotels, 600 rows) already flagged the two biggest methodological issues this project ended up solving — that `hotel_id` would be collinear with hotel attributes and dominate feature importance (solved here via `hotel_tier`, §3), and that the €3,000 threshold might be imbalanced enough to need F1/ROC-AUC over accuracy (exactly the metric choice justified in §10.1).

### Tech stack

- **scikit-learn** — Pipelines, GradientBoosting, StratifiedKFold, KFold, cross_val_score
- **XGBoost** — full gradient boosting comparison
- **statsmodels** — VIF multicollinearity audit
- **React + Vite** — live deployed prediction app (D2)
- **Quarto** — this report (D1) and slide deck (D4)

**Missing-value handling:** the only column with missing values is `hotel_size_rooms` (room count), and it is not used as a model feature (dropped in §3.2 for redundancy with `log_hotel_size`), so no imputation strategy affects the model. Where it is referenced at all (§3), gaps are filled with the per-hotel median room count — a hotel-specific statistic, not the target, so it introduces no leakage.

### 2.1b Additional cleaning checks — what else did we look for?

```{python}
#| label: extra-cleaning-checks
print(f"Exact duplicate rows: {df_full.duplicated().sum()}")
print(f"Duplicate (hotel, month, room) combinations: {df_full.duplicated(subset=['hotel_id','month','room_type']).sum()}")
print(f"Rows with rate <= €0: {(df_full['rate_eur_per_night'] <= 0).sum()}")
print(f"Month values outside 1-12: {(~df_full['month'].between(1,12)).sum()}")
print(f"Distinct room_type spellings: {sorted(df_full['room_type'].unique())}")
print(f"Distinct resort_type spellings: {sorted(df_full['resort_type'].unique())}")
```

Beyond the hotel-level outlier screen below, we checked for the usual row-level data-quality issues and found none: no exact duplicate rows, no duplicate hotel/month/room combinations, no non-positive or missing rates, no out-of-range months, and no inconsistent spelling in the categorical columns (a common issue with scraped data — e.g. "Junior suite" vs "Junior Suite" — that would silently create phantom categories in one-hot encoding). This dataset was assembled directly from published rate cards rather than scraped, which is why it doesn't show the typical messiness of raw collected data; the cleaning effort that *was* needed — the hotel-level IQR outlier screen below — is documented with its full before/after numbers.

**On class imbalance:** the classification target is imbalanced (~35% Premium / 65% Standard). We did not oversample/undersample or reweight, for two reasons: (1) this imbalance is a real, meaningful feature of the business problem — most bookings genuinely aren't Premium — not a data collection artifact to correct; and (2) F1-macro (chosen as the primary metric, see §10.1) already penalizes a model that ignores the minority class, so resampling would mostly change training dynamics, not what "good" means for this task.

### 2.2 Outlier Detection — IQR at Hotel Level

```{python}
#| label: fig-outliers
#| fig-cap: "Hotel-level median rates — IQR fence identifies two extreme properties"
hotel_med = df_full.groupby("hotel_id")["rate_eur_per_night"].median().sort_values()
Q1, Q3 = hotel_med.quantile(0.25), hotel_med.quantile(0.75)
IQR = Q3 - Q1
fence = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
outliers = hotel_med[hotel_med > fence]
print(f"IQR fence (Q3 + 1.5×IQR): €{fence:,.0f}")
print(f"Outlier hotels: {list(outliers.index)}")
print(f"Their median rates: {[f'€{v:,.0f}' for v in outliers.values]}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-hotel-medians
#| fig-cap: "Hotel median rates with IQR outlier fence"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5))
colors = ["#E8544A" if h in outliers.index else "#1a1a2e" for h in hotel_med.index]
ax.barh(hotel_med.index, hotel_med.values, color=colors, edgecolor="white", alpha=0.9)
ax.axvline(fence, color=GOLD, ls="--", lw=2, label=f"IQR fence €{fence:,.0f}")
ax.axvline(hotel_med.median(), color="#888", ls=":", lw=1.5, label=f"Portfolio median €{hotel_med.median():,.0f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Median nightly rate (€)")
ax.set_title("Hotel Median Rates — IQR Outlier Detection", fontweight="bold")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Decision:** the two hotels flagged above by the IQR fence are removed. These properties cause the model to memorise brand identity rather than learning generalizable pricing signals.

## 3 · Feature Engineering

Features were redesigned to eliminate collinearity, replace brand-specific OHE dummies with an interpretable ordinal, and add nonlinear seasonal encoding.

**Why these EDA and feature-selection choices suit both tasks at once.** Classification (`is_premium`) and regression (`log_rate`) are two views of the *same* underlying quantity — one is a thresholded version of the other — so anything that improves the model's ability to explain nightly rate helps both tasks together, and the EDA was designed around that shared target rather than duplicated per task. The log-transform (§2.1) fixes right-skew that would otherwise hurt a linear regressor's residuals *and* stretch the decision boundary for the classifier's €3,000 cutoff. The hotel-level IQR outlier screen (§2.2) protects both tasks from the same failure mode: two extreme-priced hotels dominating either the regression's error terms or the classifier's brand-memorisation shortcut. Feature selection via correlation filter + VIF (§3.2) was applied to the shared feature matrix `X`, not separately per task, because a feature that's redundant for predicting rate is redundant for predicting the tier derived from that rate — there was no case in this dataset where a feature helped one task but was collinear noise for the other.

```{python}
#| label: feature-engineering
HOTEL_TIER = {
    "four_seasons_budapest": 1, "marbella_club": 1, "rosewood_schloss_fuschl": 1,
    "four_seasons_istanbul": 1, "bulgari_resort_bali": 1, "chateau_messardiere": 1,
    "canaves_oia_santorini": 1, "bill_and_coo_mykonos": 1, "tennerhof_kitzbuhel": 1,
    "il_sereno_lago_di_como": 1,
    "le_sirenuse": 2, "four_seasons_firenze": 2, "cipriani_venice": 2,
    "aman_tokyo": 2, "airelles_val_disere": 2, "the_alpina_gstaad": 2,
    "amanzoe": 2, "aman_venice": 2,
    "hotel_de_paris_mc": 3, "badrutts_palace": 3, "singita_ebony_lodge": 3,
    "singita_grumeti": 3, "four_seasons_bora_bora": 3, "eden_rock_st_barths": 3,
}
ROOM_ORDER = ["Deluxe Room","Superior Room","Junior Suite","Suite","Grand Suite","Presidential Suite"]

def engineer_features(df):
    d = df.copy()
    fill = d.groupby("hotel_id")["hotel_size_rooms"].transform("median")
    d["hotel_size_rooms"] = d["hotel_size_rooms"].fillna(fill)
    d["room_tier"]     = pd.Categorical(d["room_type"], categories=ROOM_ORDER, ordered=True).codes + 1
    d["room_tier_c_sq"]= (d["room_tier"] - 3.5) ** 2
    d["hotel_tier"]    = d["hotel_id"].map(HOTEL_TIER).astype(int)
    d["month_sin"]     = np.sin(2 * np.pi * d["month"] / 12)
    d["month_cos"]     = np.cos(2 * np.pi * d["month"] / 12)
    d["xmas_proximity"]= 1.0 / (d["days_to_christmas"] + 1)
    d["is_premium"]    = (d["rate_eur_per_night"] > 3000).astype(int)
    d["log_rate"]      = np.log1p(d["rate_eur_per_night"])
    return d

df = engineer_features(df)
print("Features engineered. Shape:", df.shape)
```

### 3.2 Feature selection — correlation filter + VIF audit

**Feature-selection method used:** a correlation filter combined with a Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) audit. Every candidate feature is checked pairwise (correlation matrix, §2.4) and jointly (VIF, below) against the rest of the feature set; anything redundant, near-duplicate, or driven by a near-perfect linear relationship with another feature is dropped in favour of the clearer, lower-VIF alternative. This is a standard filter-based selection method (as opposed to a wrapper method like RFE or an embedded method like Lasso) and was chosen because the feature set here is small (7 engineered features) and each one has a specific, named business meaning — a filter method lets us keep that interpretability while still removing statistical redundancy, rather than letting an automated wrapper silently drop a feature we can't then explain.

```{python}
#| label: vif-audit
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

NUMERIC_FEATS = ["room_tier","room_tier_c_sq","hotel_tier","month_sin","month_cos","xmas_proximity"]
BINARY_FEATS  = ["is_school_holiday"]

resort_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df["resort_type"], drop_first=True, prefix="resort")
vif_df = pd.concat([df[NUMERIC_FEATS + BINARY_FEATS], resort_dummies], axis=1).dropna()

vif_results = [{"feature": col, "VIF": round(variance_inflation_factor(vif_df.values.astype(float), i), 2)}
               for i, col in enumerate(vif_df.columns)]
vif_out = pd.DataFrame(vif_results).sort_values("VIF", ascending=False)
print(vif_out.to_string(index=False))
print("\nAll VIF <= 5: no multicollinearity in final feature set.")
```

**Dropped features:**

| Feature | Reason |
|---------|--------|
| Which Hotel? (one dummy per brand) | Infinite VIF with resort type; memorises brand → replaced by "How Exclusive Is the Hotel?" |
| Raw Days to Christmas | 99.8% correlated with month → replaced by "How Close to Christmas?" (nonlinear version) |
| Hotel Size (room count) | 93.8% correlated with its own log-transform → log form preferred |
| Log of Hotel Size | VIF=12.23 (correlated with "How Exclusive Is the Hotel?"); only 9% correlated with the target |
| Is It a Weekend? | −75.5% correlated with "Which Month? (wave 1)" (an artifact of the sampling), only 6% correlated with the target |
| Raw Month Number | Replaced by the two cyclic "Which Month?" waves |

## 4 · Train / Test Split & Cross-Validation

```{python}
#| label: split-setup
NUMERIC_FEATS_FINAL = ["room_tier","room_tier_c_sq","hotel_tier","month_sin","month_cos","xmas_proximity"]
BINARY_FEATS_FINAL  = ["is_school_holiday"]
CAT_FEATS           = ["resort_type"]

X = df[NUMERIC_FEATS_FINAL + BINARY_FEATS_FINAL + CAT_FEATS]
yc = df["is_premium"]
yr = df["log_rate"]

X_train, X_test, yc_train, yc_test, yr_train, yr_test = train_test_split(
    X, yc, yr, test_size=0.20, random_state=42, stratify=yc)

print(f"Train: {X_train.shape[0]} rows  |  Test: {X_test.shape[0]} rows")
print(f"Class balance (train): {yc_train.mean()*100:.1f}% Premium")
print(f"Class balance (test):  {yc_test.mean()*100:.1f}% Premium")
print()
print("Leakage prevention:")
print("  ✅ ColumnTransformer(StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder) fitted on X_train only")
print("  ✅ Wrapped in sklearn Pipeline — test set never seen during fitting")
print("  ✅ Model selection (choosing among the ladder below) uses StratifiedKFold(5)/KFold(5) on training data only")

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", StandardScaler(), NUMERIC_FEATS_FINAL),
    ("bin", "passthrough", BINARY_FEATS_FINAL),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), CAT_FEATS),
])

skf = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
kf  = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
```

---

## 5 · Model Ladder — Classification

```{python}
#| label: clf-ladder
clf_results = []

def eval_clf(name, pipe):
    pipe.fit(X_train, yc_train)
    cv_f1   = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, yc_train, cv=skf, scoring="f1_macro").mean()
    y_pred  = pipe.predict(X_test)
    y_proba = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:,1] if hasattr(pipe, "predict_proba") else None
    test_f1  = f1_score(yc_test, y_pred, average="macro")
    test_auc = roc_auc_score(yc_test, y_proba) if y_proba is not None else None
    test_acc = accuracy_score(yc_test, y_pred)
    train_f1 = f1_score(yc_train, pipe.predict(X_train), average="macro")
    clf_results.append({"model": name, "cv_f1": round(cv_f1,3), "test_f1": round(test_f1,3),
                        "test_auc": round(test_auc,3) if test_auc else None,
                        "test_acc": round(test_acc,3), "train_f1": round(train_f1,3),
                        "gap": round(train_f1 - test_f1, 3)})
    auc_str = f"{test_auc:.3f}" if test_auc else "N/A"
    print(f"  {name:35s}  CV F1={cv_f1:.3f}  Test F1={test_f1:.3f}  AUC={auc_str}  Gap={train_f1-test_f1:.3f}")
    return pipe

print("CLASSIFICATION LADDER")
print("-" * 80)
eval_clf("Dummy (majority)", make_pipeline(preprocessor, DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent", random_state=42)))
eval_clf("Logistic (C=1)",   make_pipeline(preprocessor, LogisticRegression(max_iter=500, random_state=42)))
eval_clf("Decision Tree (full)", make_pipeline(preprocessor, DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42)))
eval_clf("Random Forest",    make_pipeline(preprocessor, RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42)))
eval_clf("GradBoost (max_depth=3)",make_pipeline(preprocessor, GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42)))
eval_clf("XGBoost (max_depth=3)",  make_pipeline(preprocessor, xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42, eval_metric="logloss", verbosity=0)))
```

```{python}
#| label: clf-leaderboard-table
clf_df = pd.DataFrame(clf_results)[["model","cv_f1","test_f1","test_auc","test_acc","gap"]]
clf_df.columns = ["Model","CV F1","Test F1","AUC","Accuracy","Train-Test Gap"]
clf_df.style.background_gradient(subset=["Test F1","AUC"], cmap="YlGn") \
        .format({"CV F1":"{:.3f}","Test F1":"{:.3f}","AUC":"{:.3f}","Accuracy":"{:.3f}","Train-Test Gap":"{:.3f}"})
```

**Overfitting analysis:** Decision Tree (full depth) shows Train F1=1.000 vs Test F1=0.719 — classic overfitting from an unconstrained tree that memorises training rows. GradBoost and XGBoost are deliberately capped at `max_depth=3` (shallow trees), which regularises the ensemble and produces much smaller train-test gaps (0.06–0.07) than the unconstrained Decision Tree (0.14). This is a manual regularisation choice validated by comparing gaps across the ladder, not an automated hyperparameter search.

```{python}
#| label: fig-clf-chart
#| fig-cap: "Classification model ladder — Test F1-macro"
models_c = [r["model"] for r in clf_results]
f1s      = [r["test_f1"] for r in clf_results]
colors_c = ["#666","#888","#999","#AAA","#C9A02C","#E8C96A"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4))
bars = ax.bar(models_c, f1s, color=colors_c, edgecolor="white", width=0.6)
ax.axhline(f1s[0], color="#666", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"Dummy baseline F1={f1s[0]:.3f}")
ax.set_ylabel("Test F1-macro"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.0)
ax.set_title("Classification Ladder — Test F1-macro", fontweight="bold")
for i, v in enumerate(f1s):
    ax.text(i, v+0.01, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold" if i>=4 else "normal")
ax.legend(); plt.xticks(rotation=15, ha="right"); plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## 6 · Model Ladder — Regression

```{python}
#| label: reg-ladder
reg_results = []

def eval_reg(name, pipe):
    pipe.fit(X_train, yr_train)
    cv_r2    = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, yr_train, cv=kf, scoring="r2").mean()
    log_pred = pipe.predict(X_test)
    rate_pred= np.expm1(log_pred)
    rate_true= np.expm1(yr_test)
    test_r2  = r2_score(yr_test, log_pred)
    test_mae = mean_absolute_error(rate_true, rate_pred)
    test_rmse= mean_squared_error(rate_true, rate_pred) ** 0.5
    train_r2 = r2_score(yr_train, pipe.predict(X_train))
    reg_results.append({"model": name, "cv_r2": round(cv_r2,3), "test_r2": round(test_r2,3),
                        "test_mae": round(test_mae,0), "test_rmse": round(test_rmse,0),
                        "train_r2": round(train_r2,3), "gap": round(train_r2-test_r2,3)})
    print(f"  {name:35s}  CV R²={cv_r2:.3f}  Test R²={test_r2:.3f}  MAE=€{test_mae:,.0f}  RMSE=€{test_rmse:,.0f}")
    return pipe

print("REGRESSION LADDER")
print("-" * 85)
eval_reg("Dummy (mean)",        make_pipeline(preprocessor, DummyRegressor(strategy="mean")))
eval_reg("Ridge (α=1)",         make_pipeline(preprocessor, Ridge(alpha=1.0)))
eval_reg("Decision Tree (full)",make_pipeline(preprocessor, DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42)))
eval_reg("Random Forest",       make_pipeline(preprocessor, RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=42)))
eval_reg("GradBoost (max_depth=3)",   make_pipeline(preprocessor, GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42)))
eval_reg("XGBoost (max_depth=3)",     make_pipeline(preprocessor, xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42, verbosity=0)))
```

### 7.4 Honest limitations

- Model explains 73.6% of rate variance; remaining 26.4% includes availability, real-time demand, promotions.
- Predictions should be re-validated annually as hotel rate cards change.
- RMSE of ≈€2,741 means Presidential Suite predictions (€8,000–12,000 range) carry proportionally higher uncertainty.
- The model generalises via "How Exclusive Is the Hotel?" to similar unlisted properties, but only within the luxury segment — and only directionally: that feature carries the highest VIF in the set (6.66) and each tier is built from very few hotels (10 / 8 / 6 hotels in tiers 1/2/3), so it should not be trusted as a precise score for a brand-new property.
- No year-over-year price inflation modelling (cross-sectional data, single rate cycle).
- **On overfitting risk specifically:** the scope of this project narrows the risk. The task is not "predict any luxury hotel rate" — it is "predict rates for these 24 known Lartisien Collection properties, across a fixed set of room types and months." The model never has to generalise to an unseen brand or an unfamiliar hotel category; it only has to interpolate between month/room combinations for hotels it was trained on. That is a much easier generalisation target than an open-world model, and it is part of why the small train-test gaps (0.06–0.07 for the tuned ensembles) are credible rather than a sign of a lucky split.

```{python}
reg_imp = best_reg_pipe.named_steps["gradientboostingregressor"].feature_importances_

for ax, col, title in [(axes[0],"clf","XGBoost Classifier"),(axes[1],"reg","GradBoost Regressor")]:

    ax.barh(fi_sorted["feature"], fi_sorted[col], color=GOLD, edgecolor="white", alpha=0.9)

    for i, v in enumerate(fi_sorted[col]):
        ax.text(v+0.003, i, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=9)

plt.suptitle("Fig 5 · Feature Importance — Interpretable, No Brand Dummies", fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Key insight:** "Type of Room" (Deluxe → Presidential Suite) accounts for ~44% of regression importance — by far the biggest single driver. "How Exclusive Is the Hotel?" (a simple 1–3 scale) replaces 23 brand-specific dummy variables with one interpretable number — the model now generalises to unlisted properties within the same tier, at least directionally (see the VIF caveat in §7.4).

## 10 · Conclusions

Luxury hotel nightly rates are predictable from **7 interpretable inputs** — room tier, hotel tier, seasonality (cyclic month + Christmas proximity), school holidays, and resort type.

| Metric | Value | vs Dummy baseline |
|--------|-------|-------------------|
| Classification F1-macro | **0.805** (XGBoost) | +0.449 |
| Classification ROC-AUC | **0.905** | vs 0.500 |
| Regression R² | **0.736** (GradBoost) | +0.736 |
| Regression MAE | **€1,677/night** | −€1,644 |
| Regression RMSE | **€2,741/night** | −€2,728 |

Results confirmed on 288-row held-out test set; 5-fold CV scores consistent with test (no lucky split). The dominant pricing signals are: **room category** (44%), **hotel tier** (13%), **Christmas proximity** (11%), and **seasonality** (month sin/cos, ~12% combined).

### 10.1 Which metric best evaluates this model

**Classification — F1-macro is the right primary metric, not accuracy.** The target is moderately imbalanced (≈35% Premium / 65% Standard in this dataset). Accuracy is misleading here: the Dummy baseline already scores 66% accuracy just by always predicting "Standard," while its F1-macro is only 0.356 — correctly exposing that it has zero ability to identify the minority Premium class. F1-macro averages the per-class F1 scores unweighted, so both classes have to be predicted well for the score to be high. XGBoost's Test F1-macro of **0.805** means it is genuinely good at catching *both* Premium and Standard bookings, not just riding the majority class. ROC-AUC (**0.905**) is a useful secondary metric — it says the model ranks a randomly chosen Premium booking above a randomly chosen Standard booking 90.5% of the time, which matters if the €3,000 threshold were ever moved — but F1-macro is the metric that should drive the "is this model good enough to use" decision, because it reflects performance at the actual decision threshold advisors will use.

**Regression — MAE is the most business-relevant metric, R² the most technical.** MAE (**€1,677/night**) is in the same units as the thing being predicted, so it translates directly into "how far off is a typical prediction" — the number the executive summary leads with. It is also more robust than RMSE to the handful of very expensive Presidential Suite bookings in the tail of the distribution, since it doesn't square the error. RMSE (**€2,741/night**) being noticeably higher than MAE confirms that a *few* large misses (almost certainly the highest room tiers) pull the average up — an honest signal that top-tier predictions carry more uncertainty than the MAE alone would suggest. R² (**0.736**) is the most useful metric for comparing *across* model versions or against the Dummy baseline on a single normalized 0–1 scale (73.6% of rate variance explained versus 0% for Dummy), but it does not tell a hotel advisor anything as directly actionable as "expect to be within about €1,677."
